demo_input.text: I love this movie because the acting was amazing and the plot kept me engaged.

beginner_explanation: LSTM is a type of neural network that reads text one word at a time and remembers important information while forgetting irrelevant details. It's like reading a story and remembering the main plot points while forgetting small details.
advanced_explanation: LSTM (Long Short-Term Memory) networks use gating mechanisms to control information flow and maintain long-term dependencies. The core LSTM cell has three gates: forget gate f_t = σ(W_f·[h_{t-1}, x_t] + b_f), input gate i_t = σ(W_i·[h_{t-1}, x_t] + b_i), and output gate o_t = σ(W_o·[h_{t-1}, x_t] + b_o). The cell state c_t = f_t ⊙ c_{t-1} + i_t ⊙ tanh(W_c·[h_{t-1}, x_t] + b_c), and hidden state h_t = o_t ⊙ tanh(c_t). LSTMs solve the vanishing gradient problem of standard RNNs.

formula_cards.title: Forget Gate
formula_cards.explanation: Decides what information to discard from the cell state. σ is sigmoid (0=forget, 1=keep all).
formula_cards.example: f_t = [0.9, 0.1, 0.8, ...] means forget 10% of info in dimension 2

formula_cards.title: Input Gate & Cell Update
formula_cards.formula: i_t = σ(W_i·[h_{t-1}, x_t] + b_i); c̃_t = tanh(W_c·[h_{t-1}, x_t] + b_c); c_t = f_t⊙c_{t-1} + i_t⊙c̃_t
formula_cards.explanation: Decides what new information to store in the cell state. i_t controls how much new info to add; c̃_t is the candidate value.
formula_cards.example: If i_t=0.8 and c̃_t=0.5, add 0.4 to cell state in that dimension

formula_cards.title: Output Gate & Hidden State
formula_cards.formula: o_t = σ(W_o·[h_{t-1}, x_t] + b_o); h_t = o_t ⊙ tanh(c_t)
formula_cards.explanation: Decides what parts of the cell state to output as the hidden state, which is passed to the next timestep and used for predictions.
formula_cards.example: o_t=0.7 means output 70% of the transformed cell state

step_explanations.title: Validate Input Sequence
step_explanations.description: Check that input text is non-empty and can be tokenized into a sequence.
step_explanations.why_it_matters: LSTM processes sequences - needs valid text to convert to token/embedding sequence.

step_explanations.title: Embed Input Tokens
step_explanations.description: Convert tokens to dense embedding vectors that the LSTM can process.
step_explanations.why_it_matters: LSTM operates on continuous vectors, not discrete tokens.

step_explanations.title: LSTM Forward Pass (Timestep 1 to T)
step_explanations.description: Process each token sequentially: update forget/input/output gates and cell/hidden states.
step_explanations.formula: f_t, i_t, o_t, c_t, h_t computed at each timestep
step_explanations.why_it_matters: This is the core computation - the LSTM 'reads' the sequence and builds an internal representation.

step_explanations.title: Generate Prediction from Final Hidden State
step_explanations.description: Use the last hidden state h_T (or all hidden states) to predict sentiment or next word.
step_explanations.why_it_matters: The final hidden state summarizes the entire input sequence and is used for the downstream task.

hover_annotations.definition: The LSTM's memory - a vector that carries information across timesteps, updated by gates.
hover_annotations.formula_meaning: c_t = f_t⊙c_{t-1} + i_t⊙c̃_t - controls what's remembered vs. forgotten
hover_annotations.example: c_t shape [128] - can remember info from 50+ timesteps ago
hover_annotations.common_mistake: Confusing cell state (long-term memory) with hidden state (short-term output)

hover_annotations.definition: The LSTM's output at each timestep, used for predictions and passed to the next timestep.
hover_annotations.formula_meaning: h_t = o_t ⊙ tanh(c_t) - filtered version of cell state
hover_annotations.example: h_t shape [128] - encodes the 'current understanding' after reading token t
hover_annotations.common_mistake: Thinking h_t is the same as c_t (it's a transformed subset of c_t, controlled by output gate)

references.title: Long Short-Term Memory
references.relevance: Original LSTM paper introducing the gating mechanism to solve vanishing gradients in RNNs.

references.title: Deep Learning
references.authors: Goodfellow, I., Bengio, Y., and Courville, A.

receiver_mode_explanations.explanation: LSTM reads text word by word, remembering important things and forgetting unimportant details. Like remembering the main plot of a movie.
receiver_mode_explanations.teaching_notes: Use a simple sentence. Show how the 'memory' (cell state) changes at each word.

receiver_mode_explanations.explanation: LSTM has three gates: forget (what to discard), input (what new info to add), output (what to output). Formulas: f_t = σ(W_f·[h_{t-1}, x_t]), etc.
receiver_mode_explanations.technical_detail: Cell state c_t carries long-term info. Hidden state h_t is the output. Bidirectional LSTM reads both forward and backward. Stacked LSTM has multiple layers.

receiver_mode_explanations.explanation: LSTM solves vanishing gradients via additive cell updates (gradients flow unchanged through additions). Still widely used, though Transformers have largely replaced LSTMs for NLP. Research shows LSTMs can capture ~100-200 timesteps of dependency.
receiver_mode_explanations.technical_detail: Limitations: sequential (can't parallelize), still struggles with very long dependencies. Variants: GRU (simpler, 2 gates), BiLSTM (bidirectional), Stacked LSTM (multiple layers).

receiver_mode_explanations.explanation: LSTM forward pass is O(T×H²) where T=timesteps, H=hidden size. Use PyTorch nn.LSTM. For NLP, embed tokens first (nn.Embedding). Bidirectional doubles parameters.
receiver_mode_explanations.technical_detail: Complexity: O(T×H²) for hidden-hidden matmuls. Memory: O(L×T×H) for hidden states (L=layers). API: torch.nn.LSTM, tf.keras.layers.LSTM.

receiver_mode_explanations.explanation: LSTM introduces gating mechanisms in neural networks. Great for teaching why RNNs fail and how LSTMs fix it.
receiver_mode_explanations.teaching_notes: Quiz: What does each gate do? Exercise: Trace an LSTM forward pass manually for a 3-word sentence. Compare RNN vs. LSTM vanishing gradient.

research_context: LSTM (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997) revolutionized sequence modeling by solving the vanishing gradient problem. It remained state-of-the-art for NLP until the Transformer (2017). LSTMs are still widely used for time series, speech, and resource-constrained applications.

teaching_notes.summary: LSTM uses gating mechanisms to maintain long-term dependencies in sequential data.
quiz_questions: What problem does LSTM solve that standard RNN cannot?
What does each of the three gates (forget, input, output) control?
What's the difference between cell state and hidden state?
classroom_demo_tips: Visualize gate activations as a heatmap over timesteps
Show vanishing gradient in RNN vs. stable gradient in LSTM
Compare unidirectional vs. bidirectional LSTM predictions
common_misconceptions: LSTM understands language (false - it models statistical patterns in sequences)
More layers always improves performance (false - can overfit or be hard to train)
